title: Bounding a Function Value with the MVT
quickIdea: If f' is at most M on an interval, the mean value theorem turns that into f(b) at most f(a) + M(b - a). This is the form GATE actually asks.
remember: From f(b) - f(a) = f'(c)(b - a): if f'(x) <= M for every interior x and b > a, then f(b) <= f(a) + M(b - a).
If |f'(x)| <= M then |f(b) - f(a)| <= M|b - a|, the Lipschitz form of the same statement.
The bound is attained exactly by a straight line of slope M, so it is the best possible bound and not merely a safe one.
With only an upper bound on f' there is no lower bound on f(b): the value can be far below f(a) - M(b - a) is not a claim.
The bound needs f' <= M on the whole interval. A bound at a single point proves nothing about f(b).

example.prompt: GATE CSE 2021 Set 2 Q.25: f is continuous on [-3, 3] and differentiable on (-3, 3) with f'(x) <= 2 everywhere there. If f(-3) = 7, how large can f(3) be?
example.work: The hypotheses are exactly those of the mean value theorem on [-3, 3], so some c in (-3, 3) has f'(c) = (f(3) - f(-3)) / (3 - (-3)) = (f(3) - 7) / 6. Since f'(c) <= 2, (f(3) - 7)/6 <= 2, hence f(3) - 7 <= 12.
example.answer: f(3) <= 19, so f(3) is at most 19. The bound is attained by f(x) = 2x + 13.

gateAngle: 2021 Set 2 Q.25 is the only verified GATE CSE question in this topic whose answer is a number, and it is a one-line application once the theorem is recognised. The distractors are the arithmetic slips: forgetting the interval length 6, or answering 12 by reporting f(3) - f(-3) instead of f(3).

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2021 Set 2 Q.25: f' <= 2 on (-3, 3), f(-3) = 7; the largest possible f(3).

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: f is continuous on [1, 4], differentiable on (1, 4), f'(x) <= -1 there, and f(1) = 5. What is the largest possible f(4)?
variations.why: Same theorem with a negative bound: f(4) = f(1) + 3 f'(c) <= 5 - 3 = 2. The variation checks that the sign of the bound is carried through, which is where the 2021 question's easier cousins usually break.

trap.what: Using the interval length of the wrong pair of points, or treating an upper bound on f' as a lower bound as well.
trap.why: The theorem multiplies f'(c) by b - a, so the interval matters, and f' <= M says nothing about how fast f may fall.
trap.counterexample: With f'(x) <= 2 on [-3, 3] and f(-3) = 7, the value f(3) = -107 is perfectly legal (take f(x) = -19x - 50, whose slope -19 is below 2 and whose value at -3 is 7). Only the upper bound 19 follows from the data.

check.question: f is continuous on [0, 4], differentiable inside, f'(x) <= 3, and f(0) = 1. Bound f(4).
check.explanation: f(4) = f(0) + 4 f'(c) <= 1 + 12 = 13, by the mean value theorem on [0, 4].
